title: Small Agent Group is the Future of Digital Health
one_liner: Use a small group of specialized language-model agents for clinical reasoning, evidence checking, and critique instead of relying on one very large model to do everything alone.
lead: Digital health systems often default to one large language model on the assumption that more weights and more data will yield better clinical decisions because larger models often raise benchmark scores in other settings. The paper argues that clinical work has a different structure. Diagnosis and care planning require several functions at once: propose hypotheses, gather supporting evidence, challenge weak claims, and keep cost and reliability within acceptable bounds. A Small Agent Group (SAG) splits those functions across a few collaborating agents and lets them deliberate before producing the answer. The reported result is better clinical performance than a single giant model, with better balance across effectiveness, reliability, and deployment cost, because the group can expose and revise weak claims before the final answer is returned.

problem.h2: Why one model is a poor fit for clinical decision-making
paras: Clinical questions are rarely solved by a single forward pass from symptoms to answer. A safe recommendation must gather evidence, compare several possible conditions, check whether the proposed treatment contradicts the evidence, and sometimes abstain or escalate. A monolithic model can produce all of these in one response, but it has no explicit internal division of labor, so reasoning errors and unsupported claims can pass through the same channel that generated the initial answer.

Scaling the model size does not remove that structural issue. A larger model may know more medicine, yet it still has to play diagnostician, reviewer, and critic with one shared state and one objective at inference time, meaning the stage when the model is generating the answer from the current prompt. That makes reliability and cost hard to balance, especially when the deployment setting needs repeated clinical interactions.

callout.html: Clinical reasoning improves when proposal, evidence synthesis, and critique are assigned to separate agents, because each role can focus on one job and cross-check the others before the final recommendation is issued.

steps.text: Use different agents for proposing a diagnosis, gathering evidence, and auditing the reasoning, because these functions pull in different directions during clinical decision-making.
Let the proposing agent produce candidate diagnoses or treatments so the group has something concrete to inspect.
Have the evidence agents check whether the draft is supported by the case data and outside knowledge, because unsupported statements must be surfaced before final output.
Use a critic agent to identify contradictions, missing tests, and weak justifications, then revise the answer accordingly.
Produce the final recommendation only after the deliberation stage stabilizes.

paras: The paper changes the unit of clinical intelligence from one model to a small collaborative system. The improvement does not come from larger weights alone; it comes from role separation and explicit review.

hidden.name: error detection before final output
paras: The central quantity is how many incorrect or weak claims are caught before the answer reaches the user. A single model can internally revise its own draft, but that process is opaque and tightly coupled to the same generation dynamics that created the draft. SAG makes the checking process external and explicit. One agent states a claim, another inspects evidence, and a third challenges the conclusion, so error detection becomes a visible part of the workflow.

This quantity matters because reliability in medicine is often less about producing a brilliant first guess and more about preventing unsupported recommendations. A smaller collection of focused agents can therefore beat a larger single model when cross-checking removes enough dangerous errors to outweigh the loss from using smaller individual models.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark stages where the group catches or corrects clinically important errors before release.

reads.html: The group wins when it catches mistakes that one model would have passed through, because explicit checking is built into the workflow instead of being left to one hidden internal process.
SAG improves effectiveness and reliability by distributing reasoning, evidence-based analysis, and critical audit across a collaborative deliberation process.

mechanism.h2: Why a small group can outperform one giant model
paras: The design works because clinical tasks contain several subproblems with different failure modes. Generating differential diagnoses favors breadth. Checking evidence favors precision and retrieval discipline. Auditing a draft favors skepticism. A single model can attempt all three, but the same response path must serve all roles, so the model can reinforce its own early mistake instead of exposing it because the draft and the review are produced by the same internal process.

Role separation changes that dynamic. When one agent is rewarded only for proposing possibilities, it can search broadly without also defending every detail. When another is asked only to verify support, it can reject weak statements without preserving narrative fluency. When a critic is asked only to challenge the current draft, contradictions become useful signal instead of something the system tries to smooth over. The final answer is therefore shaped by adversarial review inside the system, not just by initial generation.

Cost also matters. A giant model may be too expensive to run repeatedly for each review step. Several smaller agents can allocate computation to the stages that need it, so the system can afford structured deliberation. That trade can raise overall clinical quality because repeated checking often matters more than using the largest available model for a single pass.

stages.s: proposal agent drafts diagnoses or plan
evidence agent verifies support and missing facts

math.words: Combine proposal quality, evidence support, and critique penalties so the final answer is chosen for both usefulness and internal support.
symbols: how well the proposed answer addresses the clinical question
how strongly the case facts and references support the proposal
the cost assigned to contradictions, omissions, or unsafe claims found by the critic
the deployment cost of using the chosen deliberation path

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose an initial treatment plan scores 0.7 for usefulness.
The evidence agent adds 0.2 because the plan is supported by the case facts.
The critic finds a drug interaction and assigns a penalty of 0.4.
If the computational cost penalty is 0.1, the final score is 0.7 + 0.2 - 0.4 - 0.1 = 0.4.
A revised plan with lower initial value 0.65 but no interaction penalty could score 0.65 + 0.2 - 0.0 - 0.1 = 0.75 and become the final answer.

math.note: The paper's full system is not this exact formula, but this captures the reason group review can overturn an attractive but unsupported draft.

charts.title: Single giant model
charts.note: A single large model can be strong on raw capability, but it pays the full model cost for each use and lacks explicit internal review roles.

charts.title: Small Agent Group
charts.note: SAG gains from role separation and deliberate checking, so the system can raise answer quality while keeping repeated review steps affordable.

items.b: Agents can agree on the same wrong premise.
items.html: If every agent starts from the same mistaken reading of the case, deliberation may only reinforce that mistake because the checks are not independent enough.

items.b: Coordination overhead can erase the benefit.
items.html: Too many review rounds can add latency and cost without improving the answer, especially if the case is simple and the agents mostly repeat each other.

items.b: Weak role design can collapse into one-model behavior.
items.html: If the prompts for proposer, evidence reader, and critic are not sharply separated, the agents may produce near-duplicate outputs, so the system loses the intended division of labor.
Keep the group small, assign non-overlapping roles, monitor how often critique changes the final answer, and require explicit evidence support for high-risk recommendations.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a clinical question-answering workflow with three agents: proposer, evidence checker, and critic. Feed the same patient vignettes to a single-model baseline and to the three-agent system. Keep the underlying model family fixed so the comparison isolates the effect of collaboration rather than raw model scale.

Track answer accuracy, unsupported-claim rate, and inference cost, meaning the cost incurred while generating answers at run time. The demo should show cases where the proposer makes a plausible but unsafe suggestion that the critic removes after the evidence checker exposes missing support, because that is the mechanism the paper relies on.
demo.closing: A convincing demo should show SAG raising net_clinical_value by catching errors before the answer is released.
